paras: The lynching of John Tibbetts took place at Perham, Otter Tail County, Minnesota, at about one o'clock on the morning of June 9, 1882, when twenty men broke into the jail and hanged him from a ladder set against a telegraph pole. Tibbetts, a youth whose age the papers gave as anywhere from 12 to 17, was accused of murdering two men near the Red Eye about ten days earlier. Papers across the country carried it as the story of a "boy murderer" corrupted by dime novels, and several editorials used it to condemn lynching.

According to the Wadena Northern Pacific Farmer, E. Washington and Fritz Ferhbach left a farmhouse on the Red Eye on May 28 to look for land and were later found shot with buckshot, seventeen miles north of Perham by the Worthington Advance's account. Suspicion fell on Tibbetts, a farmer's son who had borrowed a gun that day and then tried to trade a watch and revolver in Perham before leaving for Fargo. An inquest returned a verdict of willful murder against him, and Sheriff S. Butler went west after him.
Butler arrested him at Bismarck, Dakota Territory, where the Tribune put his age at "fifteen years and one month" and wrote that he "should surely be lynched."

Brought back to Perham on June 8, Tibbetts was examined before Justice Rothpletz, and toward night "the propriety of lynching him was freely discussed." He reportedly confessed that evening, saying he had acted alone, and was baptized into the Catholic church by Father Buh.

At about one o'clock in the morning "twenty resolute men" broke into the jail and, after many blows, into his cell. When they seized him he said, "Don't boys, this is too rough." They carried him to a railroad track a few rods away, threw a rope over a round of a ladder set against a telegraph pole and hoisted him up, holding the crowd back with drawn revolvers.

No report of an inquest on Tibbetts or of any arrest of the lynchers appears in the coverage, and the wire account closed by predicting that "the lynchers will probably not suffer for their crime." A St. Paul dispatch of June 13 said Tibbetts's mother had urged him on, that he had planned to wreck a Northern Pacific train, and that "public feeling is strongly in sympathy with the lynching." A Chicago dispatch the same day called the story "a hoax" and said the mother had been declared insane six years earlier.

The core report was a Perham special telegraphed through Chicago, printed in full in the Yankton Press and Dakotaian and the Salt Lake Herald and cut to a few lines by the Lancaster Intelligencer and the Washington Evening Critic. Headlines such as "A Boy Murderer Lynched" treated his guilt as settled, and weekly digests into mid-June tied the killings to "vicious literature" or dime novels.

Minnesota papers were largely approving: the St. Paul Globe headed its item "More Mob Law" but observed that "for a lynching the mob was orderly," and the Worthington Advance wrote that "the lynching was well done." Editorials elsewhere were more critical: the Lancaster Intelligencer said the mob "made no mistake" about its victim but had "stained" Minnesota, and the Springfield Republican argued that lynching did not reduce crime.

Southern papers used the case against Northern critics: the Jackson Weekly Clarion called it the "murder of this child" and said Southern lynching only protected "female purity," while the Waco Examiner mocked "the brave mob of lynchers." The Memphis Appeal blamed books about the James brothers and parents who neglected their children's morals. No article in the coverage gives Tibbetts's race.

His age was given as 12, 14, 15, about 16 and 17; the Bismarck Tribune, which interviewed him, said fifteen. Most accounts placed the hanging early on Friday, June 9, though the Worthington Advance said "Tuesday morning" and the Dallas Weekly Herald "11 o'clock this morning." He told the Bismarck jailer he was not alone, but by the Minnesota account confessed to acting alone.

bases: Twenty men broke into the Perham jail, took out John Tibbetts, held for murder, and hanged him from a ladder against a telegraph pole (A4, A15, A24).

Tibbetts was hanged after 'twenty resolute men' broke into the jail and his cell, with no legal authority, as punishment for the double murder he was accused of (A4, A13, A15). No article states his race, so the case's place in a study of anti-Black violence is doubtful (see flags).

The Perham wire (A4, A13), the St. Paul Daily Globe (A15) and the Worthington Advance (A24) independently agree that a group took Tibbetts from the Perham jail and hanged him to a telegraph pole, and the Bismarck Tribune later refers to him as 'hung at Perham' (A35).

accounts.label: Minnesota press
accounts.gist: The St. Paul Globe and the Worthington Advance gave the same core story, adding that the mob was orderly, that he confessed and was baptized, and that the lynching 'was well done'.

accounts.label: St. Paul / Pioneer Press dispatch on the family
accounts.gist: Washington's brother and a detective claimed to implicate the mother and brothers, including a plan to wreck a Northern Pacific train; public feeling said to favor the lynching.

accounts.label: Chicago denial
accounts.gist: A June 13 Chicago dispatch called the story about the mother a hoax, said no such feeling existed, and said she had been declared insane six years before.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'A Young Murderer Lynched' and 'A Boy Murderer Lynched' treated his guilt as settled and reported the hanging matter-of-factly.
The Bismarck Tribune, before the lynching, wrote that 'he should surely be lynched'; the Worthington Advance called the lynching 'well done'.
The Lancaster Intelligencer said the mob made 'no mistake' about its victim but called the act lawless; the St. Paul Globe headlined 'More Mob Law' but called the mob orderly.
The Springfield Republican and the Lancaster 'Lynch Law' editorial condemned lynching generally, citing this case.
The Jackson Weekly Clarion called it 'the murder of this child' and contrasted it with Southern lynching, which it defended as protecting 'female purity'.
The Waco Examiner mocked 'the brave mob of lynchers' while calling the boy 'a child monster'.

conflicts.note: The Bismarck Tribune, which interviewed him, gave 'fifteen years and one month'; the local Wadena paper said about 16; the main wire said 17.
The first three agree on the night of June 8-9; the '11 o'clock' and 'Tuesday' versions appear to be garbled, since the same Worthington article has him captured on Tuesday.
